milestones.title: Stanley founds Léopoldville station
milestones.detail: Henry Morton Stanley set up a station on a hill above Ngaliema Bay for the International Association of the Congo and named it after King Leopold II. It stood beside existing Teke trading villages, including Ntamo and Nshasa.
milestones.source: Kapagama & Waterhouse (2009), Crisis States Working Paper 53, p. 2, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/57a08b46e5274a31e0000a8a/WP53.2.pdf

milestones.title: Railway from Matadi reaches Léopoldville
milestones.detail: The portage railway around the Livingstone Falls linked the river port to the sea port of Matadi. Goods no longer had to be carried by porters, and the settlement began to grow quickly.
milestones.source: Kapagama & Waterhouse (2009), Crisis States Working Paper 53, p. 3, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/57a08b46e5274a31e0000a8a/WP53.2.pdf

milestones.title: Geometric town plan and first major expansion
milestones.detail: Around 1910 Léopoldville was laid out on a geometric plan and gained new buildings such as the Banque du Congo Belge and the Hotel A.B.C.
milestones.source: Marc Pain (1984), Kinshasa: la ville et la cité, ORSTOM, pp. 15-20, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Kinshasa

milestones.title: Named capital of the Belgian Congo
milestones.detail: A royal decree of 1 July 1923 moved the colonial capital from Boma to Léopoldville. The new administrative quarter of Kalina (now Gombe) was built between Léopoldville-West and Kinshasa.
milestones.source: Valérie Piette (2011), 'La Belgique au Congo ou la volonté d'imposer sa ville? L'exemple de Léopoldville', via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinshasa

milestones.title: Government completes its move from Boma
milestones.detail: The transfer of the capital was finalised on 31 October 1929, and all the governor-general's services were installed in Kalina by the first half of 1930.
milestones.source: Valérie Piette (2011), 'La Belgique au Congo ou la volonté d'imposer sa ville? L'exemple de Léopoldville', via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinshasa

milestones.title: 'Neutral zone' separates European and African quarters
milestones.detail: The Léopoldville Urban Committee set up a buffer strip between the European town and the African cité. It was meant to be 800 metres wide but was laid out at 250 to 300 metres.

milestones.title: Léopoldville gains city status
milestones.detail: Legislative Ordinance 293/AIMO of 25 June 1941 made Léopoldville a city with an Urban Committee, covering 5,000 hectares and 53,000 people.

milestones.title: Lovanium University opens
milestones.detail: The colony's first university opened in 1954, while new housing estates at Lemba, Matete and N'djili were built for workers of the Limete industrial zone.

milestones.title: Léopoldville riots
milestones.detail: Anti-colonial riots led by the ABAKO party broke out in Léopoldville in 1959. Independence followed the next year.
milestones.source: BBC News, 'Democratic Republic of Congo Profile: Timeline', https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-africa-13286306, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Kinshasa

milestones.title: Capital of the independent Congo
milestones.detail: The Republic of the Congo became independent on 30 June 1960 with Léopoldville as its capital.

milestones.title: Léopoldville renamed Kinshasa
milestones.detail: The Mobutu government announced on 2 May 1966 that major cities would take African names from 30 June. The capital took the name of the old village of Kinshasa.
milestones.source: Didier Gondola (2002), The History of Congo, 'Timeline of Historical Events', via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinshasa

milestones.title: Palais du Peuple inaugurated
milestones.detail: The Chinese-built parliament building, 225 m long and 135 m wide, was begun in 1975 and inaugurated by Mobutu on 19 May 1979.

milestones.title: Looting by unpaid soldiers
milestones.detail: In September 1991 unpaid soldiers rioted and looted in the city. It was the low point of a long decline in which foreign businesses left and roads and services decayed.

milestones.title: Stade des Martyrs opens
milestones.detail: The 80,000-seat national stadium, built with Chinese aid from 1988 and first called Stade Kamanyola, opened on 14 September 1994.

milestones.title: Kabila's forces take the capital
milestones.detail: In May 1997, at the end of the First Congo War, Laurent-Désiré Kabila's rebel forces took control of Kinshasa after Mobutu fled into exile.

milestones.title: Kinshasa Financial Center inaugurated
milestones.detail: The Turkish-built complex of ministry towers in Gombe, begun in 2022, was inaugurated on 19 December 2023.

notes: Start date: 1881 is the founding of Stanley's Léopoldville station and is the date local historians use. The site was not empty: the Teke (Tio) trading villages of Ntamo (Kintambo) and Nshasa stood on the Pool before 1881 (Vansina 1973), and an unsourced Wikipedia passage gives Nshasa about 5,000 and Ntamo under 3,000 people; Trapido (2016) says the pre-colonial 'proto-city' may have held up to 30,000. None of these is a count, so no point is given for 1881 and the series starts in 1909. Population before 1950 is thin and uneven: seven points, all colonial administrative counts or rounded estimates. Kapagama & Waterhouse state that nobody knows the population before 1908. The 1925-1945 figures come from one table (Congo Belge, 1957) which does not say whether Europeans are included; Pain (1984) gives 48,088 for 1929 and the 1941 city-status ordinance gives 53,000, both well above the table, so definitions clearly differ. The drop in 1935 is in the source and is not smoothed. Capital transfer is dated 1923 (decree) and 1929 (move completed); some sources give 1926. Landmarks are very thin: only the Limete Tower, the RTNC building and the 2023 Financial Center had sourced heights, and three of the five entries are buildings of that one complex. The Limete Tower height (210 m) is widely quoted but the tower was left unfinished in 1974, so it is marked 'estimated'. Left out for lack of a sourced height: Gécamines (ex-Sozacom) building (1977), Fleuve Congo Hotel (ex-CCIC), Palais du Peuple (1979), Palais de la Nation (1960), Stade des Martyrs (1994), Stade Tata Raphaël (1952), Notre-Dame du Congo Cathedral, Sainte-Anne Cathedral, Hotel Memling (1937), Immeuble du Gouvernement (2015). CTBUH lists only the RTNC building for Kinshasa.
